# Implementation of a brief intensive education programme in quality improvement

**Authors:** Robert Potter; Siddarth Raj; Leila Quffa; Naginder Singh; Hannah Kiziltug; Tanya Hall; Wei-Lin Allen; Pratheeban Nambyiah; Matthew Heron; Cheng Ong; Satya Krishna Ramachandran

**Affiliations:** 1Cardiology, University Hospitals Coventry and Warwickshire NHS Trust, Coventry, UK | 2Trauma and Orthopaedic Surgery, The Royal London Hospital, London, UK | 3Center for Bone and Joint Health, Queen Mary University of London Blizard Institute, London, UK | 4Anaesthetics, Birmingham Children’s Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Birmingham, UK | 5Anaesthetics, University Hospitals Birmingham NHS Foundation Trust, Birmingham, UK | 6Royal Papworth Hospital NHS Foundation Trust, Cambridge, UK | 7University Hospitals Sussex NHS Foundation Trust, Worthing, UK | 8University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London, UK | 9Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 10Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 11Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

Training in quality improvement (QI) and patient safety remains highly variable despite regulatory mandates. We describe a novel, intensive 5-day experiential QI education programme for postgraduate trainees that integrates real-world observation, brief didactic sessions and workshop-based improvement work, supplemented by creative storytelling and team-based development of campaign media products. First-year anaesthesia residents conducted over 100 structured operating room observations and interviews, collected quantitative and qualitative data on distractions and presented improvement proposals that they developed to institutional stakeholders along with narrative campaign videos. Postcourse evaluations demonstrated a significant increase in trainee confidence in QI methodology and presentation, with participants valuing the experiential and creative elements over traditional didactic instruction. This model demonstrates the feasibility, reproducibility and educational value of immersive, short-duration QI training in authentic clinical settings and suggests a promising alternative to longer, resource-intensive curricula.

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Despite mandated curriculum requirements, implementation challenges persist, inducing significant variation in actual training delivery and trainee experience. Skills such as communicating change through media, navigating workplace culture and using medical storytelling are increasingly recognised as essential to the successful implementation of quality improvement (QI) projects—yet they remain largely absent from traditional QI training.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- This article outlines an intensive 5-day experiential learning model for QI education, incorporating real-world application in a high-risk clinical setting and novel teaching methods, including the use of audio-visual media to develop campaign products for change by course-end.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- Postgraduate trainee confidence in QI tools and methodology improved through a focused 5-day education programme. Creative teaching methods and medical storytelling significantly enhanced learner engagement. Experiential learning can be delivered safely even in high-risk clinical environments that align with trainees’ everyday practice. The programme holds the promise of providing significant value to organisations through participants’ observations and summary findings.

## Introduction

Training in quality improvement (QI) and patient safety is a mandated component of medical workforce training, as defined by several key training and healthcare regulatory bodies, including the General Medical Council in the UK and the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education in the USA.1 2 However, implementation challenges persist, including time constraints, resource limitations and competing academic or clinical demands, inducing significant variation in actual training delivery and trainee experience.36

High-risk environments (eg, the operating or resuscitation room) may not be set up for concurrent QI training,4 and anaesthesia trainee schedules may limit the scope of team-based QI training. However, experiential learning methods are superior to traditional didactic teaching in demonstrating QI principles in practice.5 7 8 Simulation effectively facilitates experiential learning in teaching human factors theory,8 9 but resource constraints limit its broader use. In contrast to simulation and didactic teaching, observation and problem solving grounded in real-world practice offer clear benefits for identifying issues and providing direct applicability to postgraduate trainees.

Finally, as our understanding of effective QI evolves, so too must the curricular approach. Skills such as communicating change through media, navigating workplace culture and using medical storytelling are increasingly recognised as essential to the successful implementation of QI projects—yet they remain largely absent from traditional QI curricula.1012

This article outlines an intensive 5-day experiential learning model for QI education that incorporates real-world application in a high-risk clinical setting and novel teaching methods.

## Methods

### Curriculum overview

The QI education programme took place over 5 days at the programme site hospital and involved first-year anaesthesia residents. Three UK-based trainees from various disciplines also participated through a scholarship scheme. Five US-based QI and patient safety scholars (anaesthesia consultants) delivered the course (figures1 2) alongside one course director.

*Figure 1: A visual outline of the programme, which had two major design elements—lectures and workshops that provided the theoretical foundation for QI methods and an experiential learning component that allowed participants to apply these methods. QI, quality improvement; OR, operating room.*

*Figure 2: Sample schedule. QI, quality improvement; OR, operating room.*

The intended learning objectives were to give early-stage postgraduate trainees a foundation in safety science, QI methods and a real-world demonstration of these principles in their usual clinical environment, the operating room (OR). The course facilitators identified this year’s theme as ‘distractions within the OR’. Before starting, learners received precourse reading material on both QI methods and current evidence on intraoperative distractions.

### QI project

A key element of the programme involved implementing an improvement project to identify and address distractions at key safety points in the OR. Participants performed over 100 observations in 40 ORs across two main hospital campuses. They collected quantitative data on the frequency of distractions occurring between patient arrival and surgical incision, including the anaesthetic induction and WHO safety time-out phases, using predeveloped observation and interview instruments on the Hospital System’s Microsoft Forms app. During these observations, they also recorded average, maximum and minimum noise levels (in decibels) using applications installed on their personal devices from the iOS or Google app stores (NIOSH app for iOS and Sound metre for Android). These apps did not save sound recordings; instead, they produced reports of noise exposure during the 5 min measurement periods. Participants also conducted qualitative surveys of over 50 multidisciplinary team members in the OR (eg, surgeons, anaesthesiologists and scrub nurses) about their perceptions of distractions, current mitigation practices and suggestions for improvement. IRB approval was not sought for these exercises as they were primarily for local education and provided inputs to local leadership for possible further investigation or interventions.

Following data collection, participants worked in teams to develop Ishikawa diagrams and process maps to identify potential contributory or causal factors. Subsequent sessions involved supervised group discussion of the data, generation and evaluation of possible solutions, and coaching on the optimal presentation of the project to an audience with the aim of influencing the culture of safety. The week ended with a multihospital presentation of the project to all key stakeholders, after which the patient safety committee discussed potential implementation solutions. Throughout the project, course faculty provided supervision and guided learners through data collection, stakeholder interviews and data analysis.

### Creative storytelling

An innovative element of this course was the production of a 5 min campaign video to accompany the data presentation. Participants were required to write, direct and produce videos incorporating elements of medical storytelling to engage audience members. Participants received instruction in medical storytelling and effective media messaging and were encouraged to apply these lessons to video production. Filming and editing were done with smartphone cameras and freely available editing software (eg, iMovie on Mac) at vacant hospital locations.

### Evaluation and survey methods

We conducted pre and postcourse evaluation surveys using predeveloped tools on Microsoft Forms. Questions included confidence in QI methods, data analysis, presentation and leadership of QI projects. Following the programme, participants received the same questions to assess the perceived effectiveness of the project they had undertaken and changes in confidence in QI principles. Anonymised survey responses facilitated honest course feedback and helped reduce potential biases. Daily debrief sessions were conducted at the end of each day to adjust didactic teaching or workshop activities to the group’s preferred learning style and to capture areas for ongoing programme improvement.

Pre and poststudy data were unpaired to protect anonymity. The distribution of responses from the cohort was analysed using the χ2 test. Pre and postcourse data were evaluated across three categories (high value or confidence, neutral and low value or confidence). Finally, participants were encouraged to provide free-text feedback for thematic review based on keywords and meaning. There was no patient or public involvement.

## Results

Of the 19 candidates who undertook the QI education week, seven (36.8%) had some prior QI experience. However, on average, most respondents did not feel confident in any of the QI domains.

Following the course, 16 of the 19 participants provided feedback (84% completion rate). Compared with precourse data (table 1), confidence scores were significantly higher for both QI methodology and the presentation of QI data (p<0.001 and 0.004, respectively). Participants strongly perceived their QI project as effective, with 13 out of 16 (81.3%) respondents describing it as valuable or highly valuable.

From the thematic analysis (table 2), the most positively received themes were a focus on creativity in communicating their QI project and their increased practical knowledge of QI methods. Candidates felt most negatively about the time spent learning QI methodology in a lecture-based didactic setting, suggesting that the experiential element of this course was relatively more valued.

## Discussion

Participants completed basic training and a predefined QI project within 5 days. For postgraduate training programmes with competing demands for time and attention, this focused approach offers a practical and efficient solution.7 While this study does not directly compare delivery models, our findings provide feasibility data. The international programme team provided richer, iterative inputs into curriculum design and delivery, creating a generalisable syllabus framework for wider implementation across the NHS and US educational bodies.

The majority of anaesthesia training occurs in high-risk settings with a strong emphasis on acquiring technical and non-technical skills. However, the dispersed nature of clinical work in ORs limits opportunities for team-based QI learning to lectures and simulation drills. Conducting the QI project within the OR offered several educational advantages. First, it retained relevance to anaesthesia residents’ clinical context. Second, collecting real-world (vs simulated) data enhanced the validity of the findings and allowed participants to observe human factor principles in action. Third, observing care without interruption allowed broader reflection on their own clinical practice. Ultimately, the programme effectively demonstrates the feasibility of implementing QI education in high-risk environments without compromising patient care, setting an important precedent for future initiatives. The course underwent several iterations over 7 years, culminating in the current programme. The summary of Kern’s 6-step model13 in table 3 shows the key strategic approaches underpinning this year’s course.

*Table 3 Kern’s 6-step model to describe QI education-week programme implementation*

| Problem identification | Distractions in the operating room contribute to substantial patient safety risks and perioperative complicationsHybrid educational programmes (didactic, observational and workshop) are rare, but well-received and may help improve confidence and performance of QIVision: To provide a learner experience that enhances awareness of a safety or quality issue in real-world settings, enhances confidence in QI methods, helps learners design and implement change campaigns and is highly rated for value. |
|---|---|
| Targeted needs | No contemporary brief intensive programme in QI educationSatisfy key ACGME CLER requirements for residencyCreate a learning team to enhance the culture of safety |
| Goals and objectives | Design course content and choose a safety/quality topic to align with organisational goals and learning scopeParticipants will experience and practise key QI skills during the 5-day course: evaluate a perioperative quality or safety issue, conduct a deep investigation into the problem, synthesise and analyse data collected, design solutions using QI tools, communicate the findings and create a campaign for change |
| Educational strategy | Keep learner engagement high through a balance of didactics, workshops, observational/survey/interview skills and workshop-based development of final course products.Time—dedicated elective time during internship for learners and academic professional development time for instructorsCosts—internally managed, three funded participants from the UKEnsure broad and deep exposure to key concepts in QISet, communicate and maintain learning goals, objectives, and expectations |
| Implement | PDSA modelIterative improvements day-on-day of each course and year-on-year for the programmeTopics chosen to suit learner needs and short timeframeUse feedback sessions and debriefs to identify needs |
| Evaluate and feedback | Quality of final presentation materials after the 5-day course.Improvement mindset—evaluate daily and pre–post learner feedback incorporated into the next day’s approach, including tailoring lecture times and workshop elementsEvaluation of verbal feedback from the external audiences at presentations |

Participants responded positively to the creative elements such as storytelling and media. While these interventions are not unique in QI, their inclusion in formal QI education curricula and syllabi is relatively uncommon.10 14 These methods support learner engagement and provide a significant advantage—as members of a large segment of the intended audience for change, learners have reliably brought relevant design insights into the messaging style and content. These advantages are relatively untapped in organisations and reflect potential opportunities for improving the likelihood of change uptake.15 This study’s limitations include the single-centre design, small sample size, unpaired pre and postcourse data, self-reported CIs and lack of long-term follow-up. These highlight the need to evaluate the generalisability of such programmes across broader settings (eg, foundation schools in the NHS and national QI curricula) and longer term outcomes, including the future likelihood of using design thinking, QI methods and creative storytelling for more effective provider engagement.

## Conclusion

Postgraduate trainee confidence in QI tools and methodology improved through a focused, 5-day education programme. Creative teaching methods and experiential learning significantly enhanced learner engagement, when delivered in high-risk clinical environments that align with anaesthesia trainees’ practice. The programme holds the promise of delivering significant value to organisations through participants’ observations, engagement and summary findings.

## Data availability statement

All data relevant to the study are included in the article or uploaded as supplementary information.
